O recorte é o núcleo hiperárido do Ataca: The study area is the hyperarid core of the Atacama, near the former Yungay nitrate mine, the most studied spot in the desert, with published climate and soil records. It rains about 0.6 mm per year on average, and the saline, oxidizing soil accumulates perchlorate at levels comparable to those measured by the Phoenix lander on Mars. With some of the highest UV on Earth and rare, patchy life, it has become a proving ground for instruments and rovers that look for organic molecules and signs of life. The similarity is in aridity and soil chemistry: the pressure is about 125 times that of Jezero, the air has oxygen and the surface is much warmer.

Haughton é uma cratera de impacto inteir: Haughton is an intact 23 km impact crater on Devon Island, in the Canadian Arctic, and the only one known in a polar desert. Formed 31 to 32 million years ago, it has continuous permafrost, ice polygons and thaw gullies similar to those at the high latitudes of Mars, and preserves the remains of a hydrothermal system generated by the impact. It hosts the Haughton-Mars Project and the FMARS station, where human operations with suits and rovers and the use of radar to find ice are rehearsed. Even so, it is about 40 °C warmer than Jezero and has Earth's pressure and radiation shielding.

No Vale da Morte, dois processos diferen: In Death Valley, two different processes sit side by side: the Badwater salt flat is what remains of a lake that evaporated, like the ancient lakes of Mars, and Ubehebe crater is a maar ~180 m deep, opened by steam explosions when magma met groundwater. The extremely dry climate, with about 50 mm of rain per year, and the vegetation-free terrain were used to test the Marsokhod rover (1992) and Perseverance's landing vision system (2019). For the Moon, it works as a heat test bench: the ground exceeds 90 °C, as at lunar noon near the equator. It is, however, much hotter than Mars, has occasional rain and has life.

O Vale Wright, nos vales secos de McMurd: Wright Valley, in the McMurdo Dry Valleys, is a cold, dry desert: annual means on the valley floors range from −15 to −30 °C, minimums in the region drop below −50 °C, and there is dry permafrost over ice-cemented soil less than 1 m deep, the same arrangement as at the Phoenix landing site on Mars. That makes it useful for studying and prospecting shallow ice in a Mars-like soil, from a research station occupied year-round. The soil has perchlorate, but at much lower levels than at the Phoenix site, and the analogy fails on air pressure and radiation, which remain those of Earth.

Na nascente do Rio Tinto, perto de Minas: At the headwaters of the Rio Tinto, near Minas de Riotinto and Nerva, the water is acidic (pH ~2.3) and rich in iron, and deposits jarosite and hematite, the same mineral signature found at Meridiani Planum on Mars. The MARTE project, run by NASA with Spain's Centro de Astrobiología, and the IPBSL project drilled the region's subsurface to study the life tied to this chemistry and to test technology for searching for life on Mars. The climate, however, is Mediterranean, with about 450 mm of rain per year and a flowing river, nothing like present-day Mars.

A caldeira de Askja, no planalto central: The Askja caldera, in Iceland's central highlands, brings together volcanism, ice and water in the same place: volcanic terrain, an active geothermal area, the caldera lake and a neighboring glacier, Dyngjujökull. Its lava fields were used for the field geology training of the Apollo astronauts in 1965 and 1967, and today help in studying how volcanism, heat and water interact. The analogy fails on climate: snow, rain and freeze–thaw cycles weather the rocks in a way that does not exist on the Moon, and access to the highlands is only seasonal.

O Domo de Vargeão, em Santa Catarina, é: The Vargeão Dome, in Santa Catarina, is an impact crater about 12 km across, opened in the basalt flows of the Serra Geral Formation, in the Paraná Basin. It is one of only two craters on Earth in well-exposed basalt, the same rock as much of the crust of Mars and the lunar maria. The impact reactivated a hydrothermal system that altered the basalt breccias and formed iron oxides, an environment of interest in the search for ancient habitats on Mars. The humid subtropical climate, with about 1,750 mm of rain per year, however, erodes the structure, and it has no use as a crewed analog.

O Domo de Araguainha, na divisa entre Ma: The Araguainha Dome, on the border between Mato Grosso and Goiás, is the largest and best-exposed impact structure in South America, about 40 km across. It is a complex crater, with a peak ring, breccias and impact-melted rocks, the kind of crater that dominates the surface of the Moon and Mars; that makes it useful for studying impact geology and training sample collection. It also has a sandstone cave. The tropical climate, with about 1,360 mm of rain per year, alters and erodes the rocks, and the hydrothermal alteration still needs to be verified.

Os Lençóis Maranhenses formam um grande: The Lençóis Maranhenses form a large field of barchan and barchanoid dunes, up to 30 m high, the same kind of crescent dune that covers areas of Mars. A dune model with an exposed water table reproduces the shape and size of the Lençóis dunes, and laboratory experiments with barchans seek to predict the evolution of both these and the Martian dunes. The freshwater lagoons that form between the dunes in the rainy season resemble a Mars with intermittent water in the past. The similarity is in shape and aeolian process: here it rains about 1,400 mm per year, unlike present-day Mars, and the model does not yet measure the dunes.

A Toca da Boa Vista, em Campo Formoso (B: Toca da Boa Vista, in Campo Formoso (BA), is the largest cave in Brazil and South America, with more than 100 km of mapped passages in carbonate rocks (about 114 km in recent surveys). Caves are candidates for housing bases on the Moon and Mars, because the rock ceiling shields against radiation, micrometeorites and large temperature swings; the Toca is useful for training underground operation, navigation and mapping, with controlled access. The difference lies in its origin: it was dissolved by sulfuric acid, from the oxidation of sulfides in the rock itself, and by fluids rising from depth, whereas the caves of the Moon and Mars are lava tubes.

Os análogos lunares clássicos (Cinder La: The classic lunar analogs (Cinder Lake, Meteor Crater, Iceland, Mauna Kea) were chosen for the Moon of the Apollo missions: equatorial, with basalt and craters. Today's target is the Artemis south pole: ~40 K cold, ice in shadowed craters and a grazing Sun.
Contra o polo sul, esses locais caem par: Against the south pole, these sites drop to 0.5–0.6 adherence. The Moon column is led by Haughton (1.2) and McMurdo (0.8): polar places, with ground ice, a low Sun and isolated logistics.
Recomendação: para a base permanente do: Recommendation: for the permanent Artemis base, train and test at polar analogs (Haughton, McMurdo) and use the Apollo analogs only for impact geology and basaltic volcanism.
A rede cobre 13 de 15 usos avaliados par: The network covers 13 of 15 uses assessed for Mars, but only 8 of 13 for the Moon. The lunar gaps are precisely the Artemis ones: ~40 K cold, ice and water extraction from lunar soil, dust with no wind and radiation. For these, the way forward is vacuum and cold chambers, not field analogs.
O Brasil entra na rede com três papéis q: Brazil joins the network with three roles that were missing: Toca da Boa Vista (underground), Vargeão (impact hydrothermal activity in basalt) and Araguainha (large-scale impact geology).
A nota de cada utilidade é a média das v: Each utility's rating is the average of the variables that have a value; blanks are left out. Araguainha is rated 3 in U19 on impact origin alone (hydrothermal activity to be verified).
O UV da base usa uma escala 0–3 da liter: The base's UV uses a 0–3 scale from the literature; the batches use the NASA POWER UV index converted to the same scale. Low-altitude tropical sites get a rating of 3.
Rajadas de vento: todos os locais do POW: Wind gusts: every POWER site exceeds 10 m/s, so U13 Mars does not discriminate well.
